newsitem.title: USA: World Bank pushes private sector development.
newsitem.headline: World Bank pushes private sector development.

text.p: The World Bank said Thursday it was working to reinforce the growing role of the private sector in development, saying commercial activity was central to reducing global poverty.
The bank said it had recently launched a business partnership centre designed to help meet the needs of the private sector in dealing with the developing world.
This is in addition to a decision to make coordination of private sector activities between the various Bank agencies a a senior management responsibility.
"Countries throughout the world are working to enhance the role of the private sector in their national development because it is central to reducing poverty," the Bank said in its annual report.

It said during the 1996 fiscal year, which ended June 30, the bank was working in every region in the world to improve the business environment by encouraging countries to identify and overcome constraints to competitiveness.

The bank assists countries in privatising their industries and in so-called enterprise reform by providing advice and analysis, making loans for technical assistance, and in providing loan guarantees in some cases.
But World Bank President James Wolfensohn made clear that many developing countries were not enjoying huge inflows of private investment.
"Despite the explosive growth in the world economy, many countries are being left behind," he said.
He also emphasised that government-to-government aid has been falling dramatically as the large industrial countries tighten their belts to reduce budget deficits.

The private sector is making up some of the difference but it has been highly selective with 75 percent of all private investment going to just 12 countries. Those 12 are China, Indonesia, Malaysia, Argentina, Brazil, Chile, Mexico, Peru, Hungary, Poland, Egypt and Nigeria.
For its part, the bank has making increased efforts to make certain its development projects go according to plan and that funding instalments are not held up by poor planning.
In the past, the bank has been criticised for measuring its success by the amount of money it commits each year rather than how successful the projects do after going on line.
In a briefing for reporters to discuss the annual report, World Bank Managing Director Gautam Kaji said that the bank is doing much better in disbursing funds as projects progress.
"I expect a continued robust performance on disbursements," Kaji told reporters.
But the flow of funds into emerging economies has made the bank rethink its role, he said, stepping aside from some projects it might have undertaken in the past in favour of private industry.
The World Bank currently provided loan guarantees in some of the more developed countries and was trying to find ways to provide the same service in very poorest nations.
"We are looking at ways in which ... we can provide some element of comfort to the private sector in a couple of these countries," Kaji said.
